About: sliding vs toppling on a slowly tilting rough ramp

Source

Concept
Explores when each of three differently proportioned blocks on a slowly tilting rough ramp first moves, and what decides whether that first motion is a slide or a topple.
Serves
JEE / NCERT Class 11 mechanics — static friction and toppling of rigid bodies.
Inquiry
Raise the ramp slowly, watch each block for its first sign of motion, and compare what you observe across different friction settings.
Misconception
Puts common intuitions about heavier and larger blocks to the test — the cards let you commit to a prediction and then watch what actually happens.

Pedagogy principles applied

Predict before revealEach of the six cards commits a prediction before the ramp is tilted or a threshold curve is shown.
Target the misconceptionDistractors encode "heavier slides sooner / bigger holds longer"; the sim withholds masses so every such intuition must be tested, not assumed.
What is invariantThe cards ask which observed quantities stay the same across blocks and which depend on shape — the inset chart collects the evidence one failure at a time.
Operational numberstan θ and μₛ are read live; the plumb line through each COM shows where the vertical falls relative to the block's base as the ramp tilts.
Formal layer on demandThe theory curve and sliding line stay hidden until the student has found them through the cards.

Guided Inquiry

1 · Question 1

The three blocks are drawn without their masses being given, and the simulation offers no way to set them. Before raising the ramp, predict how the angle at which a given block starts to slide would change if that block were twice as heavy.

2 · Question 2

Set the friction slider to its default μ_s = 0.5. Before raising the ramp, predict which block moves first and what it does.

3 · Question 3

Leave μ_s = 0.5 and keep tilting past the first failure. Before doing so, predict how the medium block and the cube give way.

4 · Question 4

Before trying other friction settings, predict what single comparison decides whether a given block slides first or topples first.

5 · Question 5

Now set μ_s = 0.7. Before raising the ramp, predict what the medium block does this time.

6 · Question 6

The friction slider runs from 0.2 to 0.8. Before searching, predict whether any setting of it can make the cube topple.

Blocks on a Tilting Ramp

✦Learn this with the AI tutor

01

At a glance

Three blocks of different proportions stand on a rough ramp that tilts slowly up from level. The sim shows which block gives way first, and whether it slides down the slope or tips over.

What you'll learn

  • How to tell a slide from a topple at the moment a block first moves.
  • How the first-motion angle depends on the friction setting and on the block.
  • How to compare blocks of different proportions on one ramp.
  • How a chart of first-motion angles is built from your own runs.
The apparatus: a ramp hinged at its lower end and tilted by θ, with three uniform blocks. Each block has width w along the slope and height h from it; the dot is its centre of mass.

What's on screen

  • Cube, medium and tall blocks, each with a centre-of-mass dot and a dashed vertical line through it.
  • Ramp on a hinge, with a dashed scale of 10° to 50° and the current angle θ.
  • Tags that appear on a block when it gives way, naming the motion and the angle.
  • Force arrows when Forces is ticked: weight, normal force and friction.
See itLook at the tall block on the level ramp, with its forces on. Watch for: the tall block standing on the ramp at 0°, with weight and normal-force arrows.

Fixed: each block is uniform, so its centre of mass is at its middle. The ramp turns about a hinge at its lower end, and θ is measured up from level.

03

Sliding starts when tan θ reaches μₛ

On the slope, the weight has a component mg sinθ pulling the block down and a component mg cosθ pressing it into the ramp. That makes the normal force N = mg cosθ, and friction can push back with at most μₛN = μₛ mg cosθ.

The block holds while mg sinθ ≤ μₛ mg cosθ. It starts to slide when this fails, at

tan θ = μₛ, so θslide = arctan μₛ
  • The mass m cancels. A heavier block slides at the same angle, which is why the sim draws no masses.
  • Shape does not enter either. Every block has the same sliding angle on the same surface.
  • At μₛ = 0.50 this is 26.6°. Across the slider, μₛ = 0.20 gives 11.3° and μₛ = 0.80 gives 38.7°.
See itPut the cube and the medium block on the ramp at μₛ = 0.50, and raise it to 34°. Watch for: both blocks tagged "slides 26.6°", and the tan θ readout above μₛ = 0.50.
04

Toppling starts when the vertical leaves the base

A block can tip instead of sliding. It turns about its lower edge, the corner on the downhill side, once the vertical line through its centre of mass passes that corner. The sim draws that line as the dashed plumb line.

The centre of mass is w/2 from the edge along the slope and h/2 up from the base. The vertical reaches the corner when

tan θ = (w/2) ÷ (h/2) = w/h, so θtopple = arctan(w/h)
  • The normal force does not act at the middle of the base. It shifts downhill by (h/2) tanθ, and reaches the corner at θtopple.
  • This angle depends on shape alone: 21.8° for the tall block (w/h = 0.40), 33.7° for the medium block (0.67) and 45.0° for the cube (1.00).
See itTall block alone at 15°, with Forces on. Watch for: the teal normal-force arrow about two thirds of the way from the middle of the base to the downhill corner.
See itTall block and cube at μₛ = 0.50, ramp at 26°. Watch for: the tall block tipped over its downhill corner and tagged "topples 21.8°", while the cube still stands.
05

The smaller threshold decides the failure

Each block has two thresholds, arctan μₛ and arctan(w/h), and it fails at whichever is reached first. If μₛ is less than w/h, it slides. If μₛ is greater than w/h, friction holds the lower edge and the block tips.

Block (w/h)μₛ = 0.50μₛ = 0.70
tall (0.40)topples 21.8°topples 21.8°
medium (0.67)slides 26.6°topples 33.7°
cube (1.00)slides 26.6°slides 35.0°

Raising μₛ moves the sliding angle up and leaves every toppling angle where it was. That is how the medium block changes from sliding to tipping.

See itAll three blocks at μₛ = 0.50, ramp at 30°. Watch for: the tall block tagged "topples 21.8°", and the medium block and cube both tagged "slides 26.6°".
See itThe same blocks at μₛ = 0.70, ramp at 36°. Watch for: the medium block now tagged "topples 33.7°", and the cube "slides 35.0°".
06

The threshold chart gathers the first-motion angles

The chart plots first-motion angle against w/h. The rose dashed curve is θ = arctan(w/h). The cyan horizontal line is θ = arctan(μₛ). Each block fails at the lower of the two, so the curve and the line cross at w/h = μₛ.

  • Left of the crossing, blocks tip: their dots sit on the curve, ringed in rose.
  • Right of it, blocks slide: their dots sit on the line, ringed in cyan.
  • The tall block tips whenever μₛ is above 0.40, and the medium block whenever it is above 0.67.
  • The cube would need μₛ above 1.00. The slider stops at 0.80, where it slides at 38.7°, so the cube never topples here.
See itChart on, all three blocks at μₛ = 0.70, ramp at 36°. Watch for: two rose dots on the curve at 21.8° and 33.7°, and a cyan dot on the line at 35.0°.
See itChart on, cube alone at the highest friction, μₛ = 0.80, ramp at 40°. Watch for: the cube tagged "slides 38.7°", its dot on the line well below the 45° curve.
07

Where it matters

  • Measuring μₛ. Tilt a plate until a block just starts to slide. Then μₛ = tan θ, with no need to know the mass.
  • Vehicles on a sideways slope. A rigid vehicle tips when the vertical through its centre of mass passes the downhill wheels. The angle is arctan of (half the track width ÷ the height of the centre of mass), so a high load tips at a smaller tilt.
  • Tall furniture and stacked loads. A narrow cabinet or a tall stack of boxes on a sloping floor tips at a smaller angle than a low, wide one.
Go deeper

The tags report the angle at which a block first moves; what happens afterwards is drawn for effect, not solved. A tipping block is assumed to pivot on its lower edge without slipping, which is true only when μₛ is greater than w/h, exactly when tipping comes first. Once sliding, the sim draws friction at μₛ mg cosθ, using one coefficient with no separate value for motion.

08

Summary

In one line. A block on a tilting ramp can fail by sliding or by tipping, and the sim lets you find the angle at which each happens.

Key points

  • Sliding starts at tan θ = μₛ, whatever the mass or shape.
  • Toppling starts at tan θ = w/h, whatever the friction.
  • The smaller of the two angles decides what happens first.
  • The cube always slides first, because w/h = 1 is above every μₛ the slider offers.

Common mix-ups

  • "A heavier block slides sooner." The mass cancels from mg sinθ against μₛ mg cosθ.
  • "More friction makes a block more stable." It raises the sliding angle, so a block that slid may tip instead. The tipping angle does not move.

Things to try on your own

  • Set μₛ = 0.30 with all three blocks on the ramp. Work out each failure angle first, then tilt and compare.
  • Find the lowest μₛ setting at which the medium block tips instead of sliding.
  • Repeat the tilt at μₛ = 0.30, 0.50 and 0.70 with the chart on, and see which dots sit on the line and which on the curve.
